invariants.inv-match: The stack holds exactly the currently-unmatched openers, in order; a closer must match the top.
invariants.inv-valid: The string is valid only if every closer matched AND the stack is empty at the end.

predictions.prompt: Reading this character -- will the stack PUSH it, POP a match, or flag a MISMATCH?

why_it_exists.problem: Parsing nested scopes (like brackets, HTML tags, or code blocks) requires verifying they are perfectly balanced. A naive counter approach fails because `([)]` yields equal counts but violates hierarchical nesting.
why_it_exists.better_idea: Use a stack as an active memory of unresolved scopes. Push opening brackets. When a closing bracket arrives, verify it matches the most recently opened scope by popping the stack.
why_it_exists.naive_solution: Counting the number of open and closed brackets. This fails for '([)]' because it ignores the correct nesting order.

mental_model.intuition: Unresolved open brackets pile up. A closing bracket must perfectly match the one on the top of the pile.
mental_model.description: The parser scans left to right. Opening brackets are pushed. Closing brackets never enter the stack; instead, they act as triggers to pop the top of the stack and check for a match. The invariant is that the stack strictly contains unmatched open brackets in chronological order. A valid string leaves the stack empty.
mental_model.repeated_decision: Is this a closing bracket that matches the most recent unmatched opener on top of the stack?

engineering_examples.title: Compilers and Interpreters
engineering_examples.why_this_algorithm: Pushdown Automata (PDA) couple a finite state machine with a stack to parse context-free grammars like nested brackets.

engineering_examples.title: JSON / HTML Validation
engineering_examples.why_this_algorithm: The stack verifies that deeply nested objects or tags close in the exact reverse order they opened.

failure_signals: Just counting the number of brackets (fails on ordering)

common_mistakes.title: Forgetting to check if stack is empty before popping
common_mistakes.explanation: If a closing bracket arrives when the stack is empty, it means a scope is being closed before it was ever opened. This should immediately return false.

common_mistakes.title: Forgetting the final emptiness check
common_mistakes.explanation: After processing all characters, the stack must be empty. If elements remain, it means there are unclosed scopes.

recall_questions.q: Why doesn't a simple counter work for validating parentheses?
recall_questions.answer: A counter only verifies quantities, not the strict hierarchical nesting order (e.g., `([)]` would pass a counter).

recall_questions.q: What does the stack represent at any given point in the algorithm?
recall_questions.answer: The stack acts as an active memory containing all currently unmatched opening brackets in the exact chronological order of their discovery.

recall_questions.q: What are the two failure conditions during parsing?
recall_questions.answer: 1. A closing bracket arrives but the stack is empty (or the popped opener doesn't match). 2. The string ends but the stack is not empty (unclosed scopes remain).

oa_questions.question: Determine if a string of brackets is valid.
oa_questions.answer: Scan left to right. Push openers. On closer, pop stack and check if they form a valid pair. Finally, return `stack.isEmpty()`.

oa_questions.question: Find the length of the longest valid parentheses substring.
oa_questions.answer: Use a stack to store indices instead of characters, initializing with -1 to serve as a base. When a valid pair is formed, compute length using the current index minus the new top of stack.
oa_questions.approach: Store indices in the stack to calculate distances between matching boundaries.

practice.title: Longest Valid Parentheses
practice.why: Extends the pattern to use stack indices for distance calculation.

explanation:
Validating perfectly nested scopes is a fundamental problem in theoretical computer science, separating finite state machines (which can only parse regular expressions) from pushdown automata (which have stack memory and can parse context-free grammars).

The stack is the perfect tool because it elegantly handles nesting. By storing only the unmatched opening characters, the stack naturally exposes the *most recently opened* scope at its top boundary. Thus, when a closing bracket arrives, determining if it is legally positioned is an instant O(1) peek.

In compiler theory, checking nested brackets requires a memory of what was opened. A left-to-right scan can't count nesting depth; a stack gives it the memory to keep track of this state. This is exactly how a pushdown automaton (a machine with a stack) parses context-free grammars.

For advanced problems like finding the 'Longest Valid Parentheses', we use an index-stack with a sentinel value. We seed the stack with -1 to represent the boundary before the string starts. We push indices of unmatched `(`, and on a match, we compute the length as `i - stack.top()`. This technique seamlessly handles contiguous valid sequences.

hook.scenario: Imagine typing a math formula with multiple nested brackets. You need to ensure every opened bracket is properly closed.
hook.question: How can a program verify this without getting confused by the nesting?

key_points.title: Invariant
key_points.detail: Every closing bracket must match the most recently opened unmatched bracket at the top of the stack.

key_points.title: Complexity
key_points.detail: O(n) time to scan the string, O(n) space for the stack.

key_points.title: Gotcha
key_points.detail: Don't forget to check if the stack is empty at the end; leftover open brackets mean it's invalid.
